User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: I can walk you through what’s deductible, whether to itemize, how to treat the home office, and which forms you’ll likely need. I’ll also flag a few points where I need clarification to give precise numbers.

Short summary / headline recommendations
- Report your freelance income on Schedule C and pay self‑employment tax (Schedule SE). That lets you deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses (including a home‑office deduction).
- For the home office, you can use either the simplified method ($5 × 120 sq ft = $600) or the actual‑expense method (your office is 120/720 = 16.6667% of the home). Based on rent alone, the actual method will likely give a bigger deduction (see numbers below).
- Student loan interest is an adjustment to income (above‑the‑line deduction) up to $2,500 (subject to income limits).
- Charitable contributions ($1,500) are an itemized deduction, but with the information you gave, the standard deduction for a single filer will almost certainly be larger — so you’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction rather than itemize.
- You may also qualify for the 20% Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction on net business income (Form 8995); that can reduce taxable income if you otherwise qualify.

What to report and where (forms you’ll likely need)
- Form 1040 — main individual return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — adjustments to income (student loan interest deduction, half of self‑employment tax is also an adjustment).
- Schedule C — report freelance (self‑employment) income and business expenses (including home‑office deduction, if using simplified you enter it on Schedule C; for the actual expense method you calculate on Form 8829).
- Schedule SE — calculates self‑employment tax (Social Security and Medicare) on net self‑employment income.
- Form 8829 — use only if you choose the actual‑expense method for the home office.
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (unlikely here). Charitable donation ($1,500) would go here.
- Form 8995 (or 8995‑A) — for the QBI (20%) deduction (if you qualify).
- Form 1040‑ES — for making/estimating quarterly estimated tax payments if you owe additional tax after withholdings.

How to treat each item you mentioned
- W‑2 income ($96,500): reported on Form 1040. Withholding from your W‑2 will reduce estimated tax you may owe.
- Freelance income ($18,400, 5 clients): report gross on Schedule C. You can subtract business expenses on Schedule C to reach net profit (this net profit is subject to income tax and self‑employment tax).
  - Make sure you have records/1099‑NEC from clients if they issued them; even if you don’t receive 1099s you still report the income.
- Bank/broker interest ($2,100 Capital One 360 + $420 Schwab = $2,520): report as interest income on Form 1040 (you should receive 1099‑INT or 1099‑DIV as applicable).
- Student loan interest ($3,200): the student loan interest deduction for 2024 allows up to $2,500 of interest paid in the tax year as an adjustment to income, subject to income phaseouts. Important: only interest paid in the tax year (2024) is deductible on this year’s return. Clarify whether the $3,200 is interest you actually paid in tax year 2024 (or a total paid over several years). Also check whether Nelnet issued Form 1098‑E for the year.
- Charitable donation ($1,500 to Salvation Army): deductible if you itemize (Schedule A). Since you are single and only listed $1,500 in charity and no mortgage interest or state income tax, the standard deduction will almost certainly exceed your itemizable amounts; so you’ll most likely take the standard deduction instead.
- Unreimbursed expenses ($540): whether deductible depends on what they are:
  - If these are business expenses for your freelance work (supplies, travel, subscriptions, etc.), they belong on Schedule C and are deductible.
  - If they are unreimbursed employee expenses related to W‑2 work, those are NOT deductible for most employees under current law (suspended by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act through 2025) unless you’re in a few specific categories (e.g., certain performing artists, reservists, etc.). So confirm whether the $540 are freelancer business expenses or unreimbursed employee expenses.

Home office — two methods, and which likely helps you more
You said the home office is 120 sq ft exclusive and your rental unit is 720 sq ft. Business percentage = 120 / 720 = 16.6667%.

Option A — Simplified method
- $5.00 × home office sq ft = $5 × 120 = $600 (max 300 sq ft).
- Simple, no Form 8829. Enter on Schedule C.

Option B — Actual‑expense method (you use your business percentage on shared expenses)
- Apply 16.6667% to rent, utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc., to get your deductible home office portion.
- Example using rent only: rent $1,750 × 12 = $21,000; 16.6667% × $21,000 = $3,500. So with rent alone, the actual method gives $3,500 vs simplified $600 — a much bigger deduction. Add in part of utilities and internet (the business portion of those), and the actual method grows further.
- If you use actual expenses, you fill out Form 8829 and carry the home office deduction to Schedule C.

Because your rent is fairly high, the actual method will very likely give you a larger deduction than the simplified method — but you’ll need to have records for utilities, rent, and other home expenses you allocate to the office.

Self‑employment tax and related deductions
- Net profit from Schedule C is subject to self‑employment tax (Schedule SE). The tax is roughly 15.3% of 92.35% of net self‑employment income. You then deduct one‑half of the self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income on Form 1040 (Schedule 1).
- Example (illustrative — adjust after you confirm details):
  - If you take actual home office = $3,500 (rent share) + $540 business expenses = $4,040 total deductions → net freelance income = $18,400 − $4,040 = $14,360.
  - Self‑employment tax base = $14,360 × 0.9235 ≈ $13,264 → SE tax ≈ $13,264 × 15.3% ≈ $2,028. Half of that (~$1,014) is an adjustment to income.
  - If instead you used the simplified home office ($600) + $540 expenses = $1,140 → net freelance income = $17,260; SE tax will be larger in that scenario. This illustrates why the actual rent allocation is likely more favorable given your rent.

Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- You may be eligible for a 20% deduction of qualified business income from the freelance work (Form 8995). Whether you can claim the full 20% depends on taxable income thresholds, the type of business, and whether your taxable income exceeds certain phase‑out limits. With W‑2 wages at $96,500, you may still be under the threshold for a full QBI deduction, but this needs precise calculation.

Itemize vs standard deduction
- For a single filer, the standard deduction is generally substantially larger than $1,500 of charitable contributions alone. Because you live in Texas (no state income tax) and you did not list mortgage interest or large property taxes, itemizing is unlikely to beat the standard deduction. So recommendation: take the standard deduction unless you have other itemizable expenses (large medical expenses, large property taxes, mortgage interest, or much larger charitable giving) not listed here.

Recordkeeping & practical points
- Keep all receipts and records for freelance income and expenses, home office allocation details (floor plan or measurement notes), rent invoices or lease, utility bills, and receipts for charitable gifts (your Salvation Army receipt).
- Keep 1099‑NEC forms from your freelance clients and 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV from Capital One and Schwab. Even if you don’t receive a 1099, you still report the income.
- If you expect to owe tax beyond what your W‑2 withholding covers (likely because of self‑employment tax and additional income), make quarterly estimated tax payments using Form 1040‑ES to avoid underpayment penalties.
- Consider retirement contributions (SEP‑IRA, Solo 401(k)) to reduce taxable income if you want to save for retirement and reduce current tax — these also reduce self‑employment tax base in some ways and are often beneficial for freelancers.

Questions I need answered to give a precise calculation and final filing advice
1. Is the $3,200 student loan interest the amount you actually paid in 2024 (the tax year)? Or is that the total interest paid across multiple years (2018–2021)? Only interest paid in the tax year is deductible for that year.
2. Are the $540 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses related to your freelance writing (supplies/subscriptions/etc.)? Or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from your W‑2 job? If they’re freelancer expenses, they’re deductible on Schedule C; if they’re employee expenses, they are not deductible for most taxpayers.
3. Do you have utility bills (electric, internet, renter’s insurance) and their annual totals? If you want me to estimate the actual home‑office deduction, give me annual utility/internet totals (or an estimate) and any repairs/maintenance paid in 2024 that apply to the whole home.
4. Do you have any other itemizable items (mortgage interest, property taxes, large medical expenses, or additional charitable donations) not mentioned?
5. Did you receive 1099‑NEC forms from your 5 clients, and 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV from Capital One and Schwab? (If not, make sure you have records of amounts.)

If you’d like, I can:
- Run a worked example with the numbers you gave and produce an estimated taxable income and estimated federal tax (including SE tax), using either simplified or actual home‑office methods (I’ll need answers to the clarifying questions above for accuracy).
- Draft a checklist of documents to gather before you file.
- Help prepare a list of estimated tax payments you may want to make for the rest of the year.

Which of the followups would you like?
A) I’ll compute an estimated tax and show exact calculations for both home‑office methods (I’ll assume $3,200 student interest was paid in 2024 unless you tell me otherwise). B) I’ll just give a filing checklist and step‑by‑step how to enter each item on the forms. C) I’ll answer the clarifying questions first (recommended).
